claims.claim: A user interview is a research method in which the interviewer asks a participant questions about a topic, listens to the responses, and follows up with further questions to learn more; interviews are usually one on one.

User interviews provide in-depth insight into who users are, their lives, experiences, and challenges — including motivations, mental models, and pain points — which is why teams use them in the discovery phase and why they build empathy.

Interviews come in three main shapes: structured (a fixed script of the same questions for every participant), unstructured (a loose conversation that follows wherever the participant leads), and semi-structured (a prepared guide of open-ended questions with freedom to follow up), which balances depth and consistency and is the usual default for UX interview studies.

Good interview questions are open-ended (they invite stories rather than one-word answers), neutral (they do not steer the participant toward an expected answer), and single (one question at a time — compound questions overload working memory and lose detail).

Leading questions compromise the validity of interview data; questions that name a suspected cause, such as phrasing with 'because' ('Did you choose that meal because it was easy to prepare?'), make participants more likely to agree with the interviewer.

Asking participants to predict their future behavior ('Would you use a feature that...?') is weak evidence because people are poor predictors of their own future choices; interviews should ask about real, past experiences instead.

There is no golden number of interviews: qualitative sample size is determined by saturation — the point at which further interviews stop adding new insights — and for many exploratory studies a small, well-chosen sample (often starting around five or six participants, analyzed as the study runs) is enough; an experienced interviewer extracts depth from far fewer sessions than a fixed rule suggests.

Interviews are an attitudinal method: they collect what people say, remember, and choose to share, which is not always what they actually do; flawed memory and social-desirability bias distort self-reports, so knowing what users really do requires observing them or collecting behavioral data.

Good interview sessions open with easy, concrete questions — such as 'Tell me about the last time you did [X]' — because specific remembered events produce richer detail than questions about typical or imagined behavior, and because participants relax when questions are easy to answer.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many participants does an interview study need? The 'test with 5 users' rule from usability testing is sometimes applied to interviews.
positions: Some teams assume the 5-user usability-testing heuristic applies to interview studies.
Academic recommendations vary widely: one analysis of qualitative theses found samples from 1 to 95 (median 31); published recommendations range from 5 to 50.
NN/g: for many exploratory interview studies, 5 participants is too few, and there is no single correct number.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Sample size follows saturation, not a fixed rule. NN/g recommends starting with a small representative sample (around 5-6), analyzing as you go, and recruiting more only until new interviews stop producing new insights. Participant quality and interviewer skill matter more than raw counts.

sourceRecords.title: User Interviews 101
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (Rosala & Pernice, 2023, last reviewed 2026-07-15). Supports: the working definition of a user interview (interviewer asks questions, listens, follows up); interviews are usually one on one; interviews yield in-depth insight into users' lives, experiences, challenges, motivations, and mental models; interviews are attitudinal (reported behaviors, thoughts, feelings); limitations — flawed memory, missing details, social-desirability bias — and the need to observe behavior to know what users actually do; interview guides with a few well-designed open-ended questions; starting easy and building rapport; probing follow-ups ('Tell me more about that'). Facts synthesized into original prose; definition paraphrased with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: 6 Mistakes When Crafting Interview Questions
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (Maria Rosala). Supports: prefer open-ended questions over runs of closed questions; ask about specific remembered events rather than typical behavior; hypothetical questions are weak because people are poor predictors of future behavior; leading 'because' questions nudge participants to agree; compound/double-barreled questions overload participants; ambiguous questions confuse. All example questions in this lesson are original variants, not reproductions.

sourceRecords.title: How Many Participants for a UX Interview?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (Maria Rosala). Supports: no golden number for interview sample size; saturation as the stopping point where further interviews add little new insight; 5 users is often too few for exploratory studies yet the number is often smaller than teams assume; start with a small representative sample (around 5-6) and analyze as you go; experienced interviewers extract more from fewer sessions; semi-structured studies with shared open-ended questions reach saturation sooner; participant quality matters.

sourceRecords.title: How to conduct an interview
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (GSA Digital.gov resource; usability.gov's individual-interviews page now redirects here via digital.gov/topics/usability/). Supports: a model interview structure — warm-up questions, 'no wrong answers' framing, open-ended prompts such as 'Can you tell me about the last time you tried to complete [task]?' and 'Tell me more' follow-ups. Used as a corroborating government source for open-ended opening and follow-up practice. No script wording reproduced.
